analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to classify workers correctly and notify them of their status, with fines for misclassification.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in either committee or the House before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every employer to classify each worker as an employee or an independent contractor, and to give workers a written notice explaining their status and their rights, with a Labor Department webpage explaining those rights in plain language. If an employer fails to give the notice, the worker is presumed to be an employee unless the employer proves otherwise with clear and convincing evidence. The bill would make wrongful classification an unlawful act, double the liquidated damages workers can recover for unpaid wages when it happens, add civil penalties of up to $5,000 per worker for repeat or willful violations, require states to audit employers that pay unreported wages or fail to register, and direct Labor Department offices to share misclassification findings with its Wage and Hour Division, which may pass them to the IRS.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers misclassified as independent contractors gain overtime pay, minimum wage protection, and unemployment insurance coverage they are currently denied, plus a clear notice of their status and double damages when employers wrongly classify them and withhold wages. Workers who are genuinely contractors also gain, because the notice tells them what protections they are not getting and whom to call with questions.

how_it_helps.text: Employers must accurately classify every worker and give each one a written notice of their status, plus contact information for the Labor Department, so workers know which wage, hour, and unemployment protections apply to them.
Wrongly classifying an employee as a non-employee becomes a violation of federal labor law, and workers who complain about their classification are protected from being fired or retaliated against.
Liquidated damages for unpaid wages are doubled when the employer also misclassified the workers, and civil penalties run up to $1,100 per worker, or $5,000 for repeat or willful violations.
If an employer never provides the required notice, the worker is presumed to be an employee unless the employer proves otherwise with clear and convincing evidence.

States must use auditing and investigative procedures to find employers that are unregistered or paying unreported wages and imposing penalties for misclassification, and the Department of Labor must audit industries where misclassification is frequent.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely on treating employees as independent contractors bear the cost: back wages, doubled damages, per-worker civil penalties, and the cost of putting misclassified workers on payroll with payroll taxes and benefits contributions. Compliant employers face modest new paperwork for classification notices and records.

drawbacks.text: The notice requirement comes with a presumption of employee status, backed by a clear-and-convincing-evidence standard, for any employer that misses the deadline, which shifts the burden of proof onto businesses and could be costly for small employers with thin compliance systems.
Pushing firms to reclassify contractors as employees raises labor costs, which can mean fewer contractor arrangements and less flexible work for people who prefer independent status.
The bill adds new auditing and penalty requirements for state unemployment agencies and directs coordination between the Labor Department and the IRS, expanding enforcement bureaucracy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the gains are concrete: notice of their status, protection from retaliation for questioning it, and doubled damages when an employer both misclassifies them and withholds wages. The costs fall mainly on firms whose business model depends on contractor classification, plus new compliance work for everyone else. The main honest concern is the penalty default: an employer that simply forgets a notice faces a presumption of employee status that is hard to rebut, which is a heavy stick even for good-faith mistakes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Education and Workforce and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced, and neither committee took it up before the 115th Congress ended, so it died without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Takano introduced the bill on June 21, 2018, with no cosponsors.
It was referred to the Committee on Education and the Workforce and to the Committee on Ways and Means for consideration of provisions within their jurisdictions.
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that classify workers as independent contractors, including gig platforms, staffing firms, and subcontractors that rely on the practice, are better off because the bill never advanced: no notice requirement, no presumption of employee status, no doubled damages, and no federal misclassification penalties took effect. Misclassified workers are in the same position as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers that classify workers as contractors

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so there is no record of where either party stood beyond its single Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: These businesses classify many workers as independent contractors; the bill's notice requirement, presumption of employee status when notice is missing, and penalties would force reclassification or costly compliance. Workers classified as contractors lose wage, hour, and unemployment protections that employee status would provide.

Firms that supply labor through contractor arrangements would face double damages and per-worker civil penalties for misclassification, plus new recordkeeping. Workers placed through these arrangements gain wage and unemployment protections.

Industries with frequent misclassification would be targeted for Labor Department audits under the bill, raising costs for firms that rely on contractor labor while leveling the field against competitors that underbid by misclassifying workers. Honest firms and workers both gain from enforcement.

States would have to adopt auditing and investigative procedures for unregistered employers and unreported wages, add administrative penalties, and report quarterly to Labor, expanding their workload. Their interest runs with workers', since misclassification drains unemployment trust funds.
